beginner.bluf: The price of borrowing money. When you take out a loan, the interest rate is what the lender charges you for the privilege. Central banks set the baseline rate, and every other rate in the economy flows from it.

sections.head: Why it matters
sections.body: Interest rates affect everything: mortgages, car loans, credit cards, business investment, government borrowing costs, stock valuations, and currency values. When rates go up, borrowing gets expensive and spending slows.

sections.head: Intuition
sections.body: Think of interest rates as the rental fee for money. Just as you pay rent to use someone's apartment, you pay interest to use someone's money. The central bank sets the base rental fee, and everyone else charges a markup depending on how risky the borrower is.

sections.head: Example
sections.body: If you borrow $10,000 at 5% interest for one year, you pay back $10,500. That $500 is the cost of using someone else's money.

beginner.formal: The cost of borrowing money or the return on lending it, expressed as an annual percentage of the principal amount.

moderate.bluf: The price of money over time. Interest rates transmit monetary policy to the real economy via credit costs, asset valuations, and exchange rates. The entire yield curve - from overnight to 30-year - is a spectrum of interest rates reflecting different horizons and risk premia.

sections.head: Why it matters
sections.body: Nominal rates minus inflation expectations give real rates - the true cost of capital. Real rates drive investment decisions, housing affordability, and currency attractiveness. The neutral real rate (r*) is the benchmark: rates above it are restrictive, below it accommodative.

sections.head: What to watch
body: **Real vs nominal:** a 5% rate with 3% inflation is only 2% in real terms
**Term structure:** different maturities carry different rates - the spread between them signals the outlook
**Pass-through:** how quickly policy rate changes reach mortgages and corporate loans varies by country

moderate.formal: The annualised cost of borrowing or return on lending, decomposed into: real rate + inflation expectations + risk premium.

expert.bluf: The intertemporal price of consumption. The term structure of interest rates encodes market expectations for the policy path, inflation, and risk premia. The Wicksellian natural rate is unobservable but determines whether any given nominal rate is expansionary or contractionary.

sections.head: Why it matters
sections.body: Interest rates are the fundamental pricing variable for all financial assets. The Fisher equation (nominal = real + expected inflation) and the expectations hypothesis (long rates = average of expected future short rates + term premium) provide the core frameworks.

sections.head: What to watch
body: **Natural rate uncertainty:** Laubach-Williams r* estimates have wide confidence intervals
**Transmission lags:** Friedman's "long and variable lags" mean rate changes take 12-24 months to fully affect activity
**Financial repression:** persistently negative real rates transfer wealth from savers to borrowers

expert.formal: The time value of money. Fisher equation: i = r + pi_e. Term structure: y(n) = (1/n) * sum of E[r(t)] + tp(n).

beginner.bluf: When the overall price level falls over time - the opposite of inflation. While cheaper prices sound good, deflation can trap an economy in a downward spiral: people delay purchases, businesses earn less, workers get laid off, spending falls further.

sections.head: Why it matters
sections.body: Deflation makes debts heavier in real terms. If you owe $100,000 and prices fall 5%, you still owe the same but it is harder to earn the money to pay it back. Japan experienced deflation for nearly two decades.

sections.head: Example
sections.body: Japan's consumer prices were broadly flat or falling from the mid-1990s to 2013. Wages also fell, companies stopped investing, and the economy stagnated for a generation.

beginner.formal: A sustained decline in the general price level, typically measured as negative year-over-year CPI growth.

moderate.bluf: A sustained price decline that increases the real burden of debt, depresses investment via rising real rates, and can create a self-reinforcing spiral. Central banks fear deflation more than moderate inflation because the zero lower bound limits how far rates can be cut.

sections.head: Why it matters
sections.body: The Fisher debt-deflation dynamic: falling prices increase real debt value, causing debtors to cut spending, reducing demand, pushing prices lower. Monetary policy becomes impotent at the zero lower bound.

sections.head: What to watch
body: **Core vs headline:** falling energy can push headline negative temporarily - core deflation is the danger
**Expectations:** breakevens falling below 1% is the early warning
**Wages:** sustained nominal wage deflation is the point of no return

moderate.formal: Sustained negative inflation. Fisher debt-deflation: falling prices -> rising real debt -> deleveraging -> falling demand -> further price declines.

expert.bluf: Deflation is the macro pathology central banks are designed to prevent. The Fisher spiral, liquidity trap, and ZLB constraint create a nonlinear trap. Escape requires unconventional policy or fiscal dominance. Japan is the canonical case study.

sections.head: Why it matters
sections.body: Deflation is asymmetrically more dangerous because the policy toolkit is asymmetric. This is why central banks target 2% (not 0%) - the buffer provides room to cut real rates before hitting the ZLB.

sections.head: What to watch
body: **Japan's escape:** Abenomics (2013) took 10 years to sustainably exit deflation
**China risk:** PPI deflation for 18+ months and CPI near zero echoes Japan's early stages
**Eggertsson-Woodford:** escape requires credible commitment to future monetary expansion

expert.formal: Sustained negative inflation. At ZLB: real rate = -inflation, so deflation raises real rates when easing is needed. Escape: Svensson's foolproof way or monetised fiscal expansion.

beginner.bluf: Central bank promising to keep long-term rates at a specific level.

moderate.bluf: Targeting a specific yield on gov bonds via unlimited purchases.

expert.bluf: Framework pinning yields, requiring credible unlimited balance sheet commitment.

beginner.bluf: When the housing or property market crashes, builders and developers cannot pay their debts, banks take losses, and the broader economy suffers. Property crises are among the most damaging economic events because housing is the largest asset most people and banks hold.

sections.head: Why it matters
sections.body: Housing is the biggest purchase most people ever make, and property loans are the largest asset on most banks' books. When property values collapse, homeowners lose wealth, banks face losses, construction workers lose jobs, and ripple effects spread through the entire economy.

sections.head: Example
sections.body: China's property crisis (Evergrande, Country Garden) involves developers who borrowed heavily to build apartments nobody is buying. With property accounting for roughly 30% of China's GDP, the crisis drags on the world's second-largest economy. The US had a similar experience in 2008 when subprime mortgage defaults triggered a global financial crisis.

beginner.formal: A severe decline in property values leading to widespread developer defaults, bank losses, and economic contraction.

moderate.bluf: Property crises are the most financially destructive macro events because of the leverage involved. Real estate is the largest collateral class in any banking system - a 20-30% decline in values can wipe out bank equity and trigger a credit crunch that takes years to resolve.

sections.head: Why it matters
sections.body: Property cycles are credit cycles. The boom phase features rising collateral values supporting more lending supporting more buying. The bust reverses this: falling values trigger margin calls, forced sales, tighter lending standards, and a negative wealth effect on consumption.

sections.head: What to watch
body: **Loan-to-value ratios:** higher LTVs at peak mean faster transmission to bank losses
**Developer leverage:** pre-sale models (China) create liquidity mismatches that accelerate the crisis
**Wealth effect:** housing wealth has a larger marginal propensity to consume than equity wealth

moderate.formal: A systemic decline in real estate valuations leading to developer insolvency, banking stress, and credit contraction. Property-driven recessions are roughly 2x deeper and longer than non-property recessions.

expert.bluf: Property crises are balance sheet recessions with the longest resolution times. The Koo framework applies: the private sector shifts from profit maximisation to debt minimisation, rendering monetary policy ineffective. The collateral channel (Bernanke-Gertler financial accelerator) amplifies the downturn nonlinearly.

sections.head: Why it matters
sections.body: The financial accelerator makes property crises self-reinforcing: falling collateral values tighten borrowing constraints, forcing asset sales that further depress values. Resolution requires public sector balance sheet expansion or prolonged deleveraging.

sections.head: What to watch
body: **Credit-to-GDP gap:** BIS measure - readings above +10pp have preceded every major property crisis
**Household debt-to-income:** the binding constraint on recovery
**NPL recognition:** delayed recognition prolongs the crisis but smooths the initial shock

expert.formal: Systemic property collapse triggering the Bernanke-Gertler financial accelerator: falling collateral -> tighter credit -> forced deleveraging -> further price declines. Resolution: 5-10 years in advanced economies.

beginner.bluf: Central bank charges banks for holding money.

moderate.bluf: Deposit rate below zero to stimulate lending. Used by BOJ, ECB, SNB.

expert.bluf: Sub-zero rates via tiered remuneration; debated due to NIM compression and reversal rate.

beginner.bluf: Rates at zero but nobody borrows or spends.

moderate.bluf: Monetary policy loses effect at zero rates.

expert.bluf: IS curve at ZLB; requires expected inflation, fiscal expansion, or structural reform.

beginner.bluf: Central banks moving in opposite directions.

moderate.bluf: Major CBs pursuing different policies, creating rate differentials.

expert.bluf: Cross-CB differentials driving FX/carry/flows. Current: Fed hold vs ROW easing.

beginner.bluf: Negative Interest Rate Policy.

moderate.bluf: Unconventional sub-zero rates to combat deflation.

expert.bluf: Sub-zero exploiting ELB; transmission impaired by bank profitability compression.

beginner.bluf: When a borrowing boom suddenly collapses.

moderate.bluf: Speculative excess leading to forced selling as leverage unwinds.

expert.bluf: Phase transition from Ponzi finance to Fisherian debt deflation.

beginner.bluf: Extra return for locking money in long-term bonds.

moderate.bluf: Compensation for long-term bond holding. ACM/Kim-Wright models.

expert.bluf: Beyond expected short rates; re-emerging from post-QE suppression.

beginner.bluf: Personal Consumption Expenditures - the Federal Reserve's preferred way to measure inflation in the US.

moderate.bluf: Price index measuring consumer spending. Core PCE (ex food/energy) is the Fed's preferred inflation gauge. Uses Fisher-ideal weighting, typically runs 30-40bps below CPI.

expert.bluf: Chain-weighted Fisher-ideal index with broader scope than CPI (includes employer-paid healthcare, imputed financial services). Substitution bias lower than CPI. 'Supercore' (core services ex-housing) is the current focus for persistence assessment.

beginner.bluf: Purchasing Managers' Index - a monthly survey that shows whether businesses are growing or shrinking. Above 50 means growth.

moderate.bluf: Diffusion index from business surveys. Above 50 = expansion, below 50 = contraction. Manufacturing and services PMIs are leading indicators. Key providers: S&P Global (Markit), ISM.

expert.bluf: Diffusion index with leading indicator properties - typically leads GDP by 1-2 quarters. New orders-to-inventory ratio is the most forward-looking sub-component. Cross-country PMI divergence signals trade flow and FX implications.

beginner.bluf: Producer Price Index - measures price changes from the seller's perspective, before goods reach consumers.

moderate.bluf: Measures wholesale/producer-level price changes. Leads CPI as cost pressures pass through the supply chain. Negative PPI signals overcapacity or weak demand.

expert.bluf: Input cost gauge; PPI-CPI spread indicates margin pressure or pass-through dynamics. In China, persistent PPI deflation signals overcapacity and is deflationary for global goods prices via export channel.

beginner.bluf: Quantitative Easing - when a central bank creates new money to buy government bonds, pushing interest rates down and encouraging spending.

moderate.bluf: Unconventional monetary policy: central bank purchases government bonds (and sometimes corporate bonds) to lower long-term rates and ease financial conditions when policy rates are near zero.

expert.bluf: Large-scale asset purchases operating through portfolio balance (duration extraction), signalling, and wealth channels. Stock vs flow debate: purchases vs holdings. Effectiveness diminishes with scale; reversal rate and market functioning concerns constrain the envelope.

beginner.bluf: Quantitative Tightening - the opposite of QE. The central bank lets bonds it owns mature without replacing them, pulling money out of the system.

moderate.bluf: Reverse of QE: central bank shrinks its balance sheet by not reinvesting maturing bonds. Reduces reserves in the banking system and increases duration supply for private markets to absorb.

expert.bluf: Balance sheet normalisation via passive runoff or active sales. Increases net duration supply, pressuring term premium upward. Reserve drain dynamics nonlinear - 'ample to scarce' transition is the key risk (cf. Sept 2019 repo spike). Currently running at ~$60bn/month for the Fed.

beginner.bluf: Effective Lower Bound - the lowest interest rate a central bank can realistically go to. Near zero, or slightly below.

moderate.bluf: The practical minimum for policy rates. Slightly below zero (cash storage costs create a small buffer), but deep negative rates impair bank profitability. Constrains conventional monetary policy.

expert.bluf: Operational floor below which rate cuts become counterproductive via NIM compression and the 'reversal rate' (Brunnermeier & Koby). Estimated at -50 to -100bps depending on banking system structure. Motivates unconventional tools: QE, forward guidance, YCC.

beginner.bluf: Overnight Index Swap - a financial contract used to bet on or hedge against future central bank interest rate decisions.

moderate.bluf: Swap where fixed rate is exchanged for compounded overnight rate (SOFR, SONIA, etc.). OIS curve is the market's pricing of expected central bank rate path.

expert.bluf: Fixed-for-floating swap referencing overnight benchmark. OIS-Treasury spread is a funding stress gauge. OIS curve extraction provides clean rate expectations stripping out term premium and credit risk present in government bond yields.

beginner.bluf: Medium-term Lending Facility - one of the main tools China's central bank uses to provide money to banks and signal its policy direction.

moderate.bluf: PBOC's primary medium-term liquidity tool (typically 1-year maturity). The MLF rate serves as the anchor for the Loan Prime Rate (LPR), making it the de facto policy rate.

expert.bluf: 1Y facility providing medium-term liquidity to banks; rate acts as the policy signal anchor for LPR pricing. PBOC can adjust volume and rate independently, allowing nuanced policy calibration. MLF-LPR transmission is the primary monetary policy channel in China.

beginner.bluf: Reserve Requirement Ratio - the percentage of deposits that Chinese banks must keep in reserve. Cutting it frees up money for lending.

moderate.bluf: Percentage of deposits banks must hold as reserves with the central bank. PBOC uses RRR cuts as a blunt liquidity tool - each 25bp cut releases ~¥500bn. Currently around 7.4% for large banks.

expert.bluf: Quantitative tool releasing base money; each 50bp cut ≈ ¥1tn liquidity injection. Unlike rate cuts, RRR changes affect the money multiplier and total credit capacity. PBOC uses RRR asymmetrically - differential requirements by bank size and lending targets.

beginner.bluf: Cyclically Adjusted Primary Balance - a measure of government finances that strips out the effects of economic booms and busts to show the underlying fiscal position.

moderate.bluf: Fiscal balance adjusted for the economic cycle and excluding interest payments. Isolates discretionary fiscal policy from automatic stabilisers. The IMF's preferred metric for assessing fiscal effort.

expert.bluf: Structural fiscal metric removing cyclical revenue/expenditure effects and debt service. Estimation requires output gap measurement (subject to real-time errors). The r-g differential (interest rate vs growth rate) determines whether positive CAPB is needed for debt stabilisation.

beginner.bluf: When a central bank tells the public what it plans to do with interest rates in the future, to shape expectations and influence the economy today.

moderate.bluf: Central bank communication about the likely future path of policy rates. Can be calendar-based ('rates will stay low until 2024') or state-contingent ('until inflation reaches 2%'). Aims to influence longer-term rates via expectations.

expert.bluf: Expectations management tool operating at the ELB. Odyssean (commitment) vs Delphic (forecast) guidance distinction matters for credibility. Effectiveness depends on time consistency - the central bank's incentive to renege undermines commitment-based guidance (Woodford 2012).

beginner.bluf: A repurchase agreement - a short-term loan where one party sells a bond and agrees to buy it back the next day (or soon after), effectively borrowing money using the bond as collateral.

moderate.bluf: Repurchase agreement: short-term collateralised lending. Seller transfers securities with agreement to repurchase at a set price. The repo market is the plumbing of the financial system - critical for bank funding, leverage, and monetary policy transmission.

expert.bluf: Collateralised money market instrument. Repo rate = risk-free rate + haircut/credit component. Market size ~$4tn (US). Fed implements policy via repo/reverse repo facilities. Repo stress (Sept 2019, March 2020) demonstrated systemic importance and reserve scarcity dynamics.

beginner.bluf: The opposite of a repo - the central bank borrows money from banks overnight, taking excess cash out of the financial system.

moderate.bluf: Transaction where the central bank borrows from counterparties against collateral. The Fed's ON RRP facility absorbs excess reserves, setting a floor under short-term rates. Peak usage exceeded $2tn.

expert.bluf: Fed ON RRP facility provides the effective floor for the fed funds corridor. Peak ~$2.5tn reflected excess liquidity from QE and Treasury drawdown. Declining balances signal reserve normalisation toward 'ample' (from 'abundant') - key for QT calibration.

beginner.bluf: The interest rate banks charge each other for short-term loans, typically overnight. Central banks influence this rate to control the economy.

moderate.bluf: The rate at which banks lend reserves to each other, typically overnight. Central banks target this rate as their primary policy instrument. Key benchmarks: fed funds (US), SONIA (UK), €STR (eurozone).

expert.bluf: Overnight unsecured lending rate in the interbank market. Post-2008 shift from LIBOR to risk-free rates (SOFR, SONIA, €STR). The central bank's corridor system (deposit/lending facilities) bounds the interbank rate around the target.

beginner.bluf: A formula that suggests what interest rate a central bank should set based on inflation and economic growth.

moderate.bluf: Monetary policy rule: i = r* + π + 0.5(π − π*) + 0.5(y − y*). Prescribes the policy rate based on the neutral rate, inflation gap, and output gap. Used as a benchmark rather than a rigid rule.

expert.bluf: Normative policy benchmark. Original (1993) vs modified (1999, with larger inflation coefficient) specifications. Operational challenges: r-star and output gap are unobservable in real time. Inertial Taylor Rules (with rate smoothing) better approximate actual CB behaviour.

beginner.bluf: The 'neutral' interest rate - the rate at which the economy is neither being stimulated nor held back. No one can observe it directly.

moderate.bluf: The neutral real interest rate: the rate consistent with full employment and stable inflation. Estimated via models (Laubach-Williams, Holston-Laubach-Williams). Currently debated whether it has risen post-pandemic.

expert.bluf: Unobservable equilibrium real rate. HLW estimates ~0.5-1.0% for US, but confidence intervals span 200bp+. Determinants: demographics, productivity, global savings, fiscal stance. Post-pandemic reassessment: structural fiscal expansion and deglobalisation may have raised r-star, with profound implications for monetary policy stance assessment.

beginner.bluf: The interest rate where the economy is in balance - not too hot, not too cold. Also called the neutral rate or r-star.

moderate.bluf: The equilibrium interest rate that neither stimulates nor restrains growth. Same concept as r-star. Critical for assessing whether monetary policy is tight or loose.

expert.bluf: Wicksellian concept: the rate equating desired saving and investment at full employment. Equivalent to r-star in modern DSGE frameworks. The gap between actual real rate and natural rate defines the monetary policy stance - but measurement uncertainty is substantial.

beginner.bluf: A central bank strategy of setting a specific inflation goal (usually 2%) and adjusting interest rates to try to hit it.

moderate.bluf: Monetary policy framework where the central bank commits to a specific inflation target (typically 2%) and adjusts policy to achieve it. Adopted by most major central banks. Anchors inflation expectations.

expert.bluf: Framework pioneered by RBNZ (1990). Flexible inflation targeting allows temporary deviations for output/financial stability considerations. Average inflation targeting (AIT) - adopted by the Fed in 2020 - allows overshooting after undershoots. Credibility is the key asset; once expectations de-anchor, re-anchoring is costly.

beginner.bluf: The point where interest rates hit zero and can't easily go lower, limiting the central bank's main tool for fighting economic weakness.

moderate.bluf: The constraint where nominal interest rates cannot fall significantly below zero. Forces central banks to use unconventional tools (QE, forward guidance, negative rates). A key challenge during the 2010s globally.

expert.bluf: Theoretical floor on nominal rates from cash arbitrage. In practice, the ELB is slightly negative (storage costs). ZLB constraint motivated the entire unconventional policy toolkit. Secular stagnation hypothesis (Summers 2014) argued ZLB would bind frequently given low r-star.

beginner.bluf: The interest rate a central bank pays (or charges) commercial banks for parking money overnight. In the eurozone, the ECB's deposit rate is the key policy rate - it determines the floor for all other interest rates in the economy.

sections.head: Why it matters
sections.body: Banks hold reserves at the central bank. The deposit rate is what they earn (or pay, if negative) on those reserves. No bank would lend to another at a rate below what the central bank pays, so this sets the floor for the entire financial system.

sections.head: Example
sections.body: The ECB's deposit rate was negative (-0.5%) from 2014 to 2022 - banks were charged to park money. When inflation surged, the ECB raised it to 4.0%, making it attractive to hold reserves and expensive to lend.

beginner.formal: The interest rate paid by a central bank on overnight deposits held by commercial banks, typically forming the floor of the interest rate corridor.

moderate.bluf: The rate paid on excess reserves, forming the floor of the interest rate corridor. In the ECB's framework, the deposit facility rate is now the primary policy rate because the banking system operates with structural excess liquidity post-QE.

sections.head: Why it matters
sections.body: In a system with excess liquidity, the deposit rate becomes the binding policy rate because banks are net depositors. The ECB formalised this in 2024. The Fed's equivalent is IORB.

sections.head: What to watch
body: **Corridor width:** the gap between lending and deposit rates defines rate volatility
**Excess liquidity:** when reserves are abundant, money market rates trade near the deposit floor
**Tiering:** the ECB exempted some deposits from negative rates to protect bank profitability

moderate.formal: The deposit facility rate forming the floor of the central bank's interest rate corridor.

expert.bluf: The deposit facility rate is the effective policy rate in a structural excess liquidity regime. The ECB's March 2024 framework review formalised this by making the DFR the primary rate and narrowing the MRO-DFR corridor to 15bp. Floor systems are now the global standard post-QE.

sections.head: Why it matters
sections.body: Post-QE excess liquidity pushed money market rates to the deposit floor, making corridor systems obsolete. The ECB, Fed, and BOE all operate de facto floor systems. Transmission to ESTR/SOFR/SONIA is near-perfect.

sections.head: What to watch
body: **ESTR-DFR spread:** should be near zero - widening signals money market stress
**Reserve demand curve:** as QT drains reserves, the system may transition back to corridor
**Tiering:** ECB's formula (6x minimum reserves exempt) balances NII protection with rate transmission

expert.formal: Overnight deposit facility rate. ECB post-2024: DFR is primary rate, MRO = DFR + 15bp, MLF = DFR + 40bp.

beginner.bluf: When a central bank gradually reduces the amount of bonds it's buying, slowly pulling back its support for the economy.

moderate.bluf: Gradual reduction of central bank asset purchases (QE). The 'taper tantrum' of 2013 demonstrated that even the announcement of tapering can trigger sharp market reactions, especially in emerging markets.

expert.bluf: Transition from QE pace to reduced purchases. Communication is critical - Bernanke's May 2013 taper signal triggered 100bp UST selloff and EM capital flight. ECB APP/PEPP tapering complicated by fragmentation risk. The flow-to-stock transition debate determines market impact magnitude.

beginner.bluf: When a central banker favours lower interest rates and more support for the economy, even if it means tolerating higher inflation. The opposite is "hawkish" - favouring higher rates to fight inflation. Markets move on every hint of dovish or hawkish leaning.

sections.head: Why it matters
sections.body: Central bank communication is a policy tool. When a bank sounds dovish, markets expect rate cuts: bond prices rise, stocks rally, the currency weakens. A single word change in a statement can move billions.

sections.head: Example
sections.body: If the Fed chair says "we see downside risks to employment" - dovish (cuts coming). If "inflation remains too high" - hawkish (rates staying high or going higher).

beginner.formal: A monetary policy stance favouring lower rates, more accommodation, and greater emphasis on employment relative to inflation control.

moderate.bluf: A policy bias toward accommodation - lower rates, more liquidity, tolerance for inflation overshoot. Dovish communication shifts rate expectations lower, easing financial conditions before any actual change.

sections.head: Why it matters
sections.body: Market reaction is driven by whether the statement is more dovish or hawkish than expected. A rate hold can be dovish (if a hike was expected). The delta relative to expectations matters, not the absolute level.

sections.head: What to watch
body: **Dot plot:** median projection moving down is dovish
**Dissents:** dovish dissents foreshadow the next move
**Language:** "some" to "many", "could" to "will" - small words carry large signal

moderate.formal: Policy bias toward accommodation. Taylor Rule: higher weight on output gap vs inflation gap. Opposite: hawkish.

expert.bluf: Dovish describes a revealed preference for accommodation - higher weight on the output gap in the reaction function. Operationally, dovish/hawkish is relative to market pricing: a 25bp cut is hawkish if 50bp was priced.

sections.head: Why it matters
sections.body: Communication is a primary policy tool (Woodford). A dovish statement shifting OIS by 20bp is equivalent to an actual cut in financial conditions terms. NLP models now quantify hawk-dove scores systematically.

sections.head: What to watch
body: **Intertemporal bias:** hawkish today but signalling future dovishness flattens the curve
**Institutional bias:** BOJ structurally dovish; ECB (Bundesbank tradition) structurally hawkish
**Credibility cost:** excessive dovishness can de-anchor expectations

expert.formal: Reaction function with higher output stabilisation weight. Measured as deviation of communicated path below OIS-implied path.

beginner.bluf: When a central bank raises interest rates or takes other steps to slow down an overheating economy and bring down inflation.

moderate.bluf: Restrictive monetary policy: raising rates, reducing asset purchases, or draining reserves. Aims to cool demand and reduce inflation. Works with a lag of 12-18 months.

expert.bluf: Contractionary stance: rate hikes, QT, and/or forward guidance shift. Transmission lags (12-24 months) create calibration uncertainty. Financial conditions indices (Goldman, Chicago Fed) provide real-time tightness measures. The cumulative vs marginal tightening debate matters for assessing policy stance.

beginner.bluf: When a central bank cuts interest rates or takes other steps to stimulate a weak economy and encourage borrowing.

moderate.bluf: Accommodative monetary policy: cutting rates, expanding asset purchases, or providing liquidity. Aims to stimulate demand, support employment, and prevent deflation. Weaker currency is a typical side effect.

expert.bluf: Expansionary stance via rate cuts, QE, or liquidity injections. Effectiveness varies by transmission channel - credit channel impaired when banks are capital-constrained (cf. Europe 2012-15). 'Pushing on a string' metaphor applies when demand for credit is absent despite supply of cheap funding.

beginner.bluf: Parts of the government budget that automatically help cushion the economy without politicians needing to do anything. When the economy weakens, tax revenue falls and welfare spending rises, pumping money in. The reverse happens during booms.

sections.head: Why it matters
sections.body: Automatic stabilisers are built-in shock absorbers. They work faster than any new policy because they are already in place. During a recession, unemployed workers receive benefits (maintaining spending) and people earn less (paying less tax).

sections.head: Example
sections.body: During COVID, even before stimulus packages, tax revenue dropped automatically and unemployment benefits rose. In the US, these stabilisers amounted to roughly 2-3% of GDP in 2020.

beginner.formal: Government revenue and spending mechanisms that automatically adjust counter-cyclically without new legislation.

moderate.bluf: Fiscal mechanisms that counter-cyclically adjust spending and revenue without legislative action. European economies have larger stabilisers (~40-50% of a GDP shock offset) than the US (~25-30%) due to more progressive taxation and generous welfare systems.

sections.head: Why it matters
sections.body: Automatic stabilisers are the first line of fiscal defence. They widen the deficit in recessions and narrow it in expansions without political delay. The CAPB strips out stabiliser effects to reveal the discretionary stance.

sections.head: What to watch
body: **Stabiliser size:** Nordic countries offset ~50% of GDP shocks vs ~25% in the US
**Deficit decomposition:** a rising deficit during recession may be entirely stabiliser-driven
**Discretionary vs automatic:** stimulus packages are discretionary; stabilisers are automatic

moderate.formal: Counter-cyclical fiscal mechanisms. Stabilisation coefficient: 0.25-0.50 for OECD economies.

expert.bluf: Automatic stabilisers are the endogenous fiscal response to the cycle, typically offsetting 25-50% of output shocks. The CAPB nets them out to isolate discretionary fiscal impulse, though output gap estimation uncertainty makes the decomposition imprecise.

sections.head: Why it matters
sections.body: In the eurozone, where monetary policy is centralised and fiscal rules constrain discretionary spending, automatic stabilisers bear a disproportionate burden of cyclical adjustment.

sections.head: What to watch
body: **Output gap uncertainty:** stabiliser estimates depend on output gap measurement, which is revised substantially
**Revenue elasticity:** responsiveness of tax revenue to GDP - typically 1.0-1.2
**Fiscal drag:** in expansions, stabilisers automatically tighten by pulling in more tax revenue

expert.formal: Endogenous fiscal response: delta(deficit) = -alpha * delta(output gap), alpha ~0.25-0.50.

beginner.bluf: A fundamental equation showing that what a country earns, saves, invests, and trades must all balance out mathematically.

moderate.bluf: The identity: Y = C + I + G + (X − M), which rearranges to show that CA = (S − I) + (T − G). Saving minus investment equals the current account. This is an accounting truth, not a theory - it must hold by definition.

expert.bluf: GDP expenditure identity Y ≡ C + I + G + NX. Rearranges to CA ≡ (Sp − I) + (T − G), linking private saving-investment balance and fiscal balance to the external position. Useful as a consistency framework but not causal - identification of transmission channels requires structural models.

beginner.bluf: When someone takes bigger risks because they know they'll be bailed out if things go wrong.

moderate.bluf: Risk-taking incentive created by implicit or explicit guarantees. Banks take more risk if they expect government bailouts. In the eurozone, ECB backstops may reduce fiscal discipline incentives for high-debt governments.

expert.bluf: Information asymmetry problem: agents increase risk-taking when insulated from consequences. In sovereign debt: ECB TPI/OMT creates moral hazard by reducing spread pressure that would otherwise enforce fiscal discipline. In banking: 'too big to fail' implicit guarantees distort risk pricing. Optimal policy balances crisis prevention with maintaining market discipline.

beginner.bluf: An economic model showing how interest rates, exchange rates, and trade interact - and why countries face difficult trade-offs between them.

moderate.bluf: Open-economy extension of IS-LM model. Key insight: under floating exchange rates, monetary policy is effective (via exchange rate channel) while fiscal policy is offset by currency appreciation. Under fixed rates, the reverse holds.

expert.bluf: IS-LM-BP framework for open economies. Under perfect capital mobility: floating FX → monetary policy effective (Dornbusch overshooting), fiscal policy crowded out via appreciation. Fixed FX → fiscal effective, monetary impotent (reserves drain). Foundation for impossible trinity. Extended by Obstfeld-Rogoff (1995) intertemporal models.

beginner.bluf: The inflation rate that the bond market expects over a given period. Calculated from the gap between regular government bonds and inflation-protected bonds. If actual inflation beats the breakeven, inflation-protected bonds win; if lower, regular bonds win.

sections.head: Why it matters
sections.body: Breakeven inflation tells you what bond investors collectively think inflation will be. Central banks watch it closely to gauge whether expectations are anchored near their 2% target.

sections.head: Example
sections.body: If a regular 10-year Treasury yields 4.5% and a 10-year TIPS yields 2.0%, the breakeven is 2.5%. The market expects 2.5% average inflation over the next decade.

beginner.formal: The difference between nominal and inflation-linked bond yields of the same maturity, representing market-implied average inflation.

moderate.bluf: Market-implied inflation derived from nominal minus real (TIPS) yields. Breakevens embed both expectations and an inflation risk premium, so they are biased. The 5Y5Y forward breakeven is the Fed's preferred gauge of long-term anchoring.

sections.head: Why it matters
sections.body: The 5Y5Y forward strips out near-term noise to reveal whether long-term expectations remain anchored. De-anchoring would force much more aggressive tightening.

sections.head: What to watch
body: **5Y5Y forward:** the Fed's key gauge - should hover near 2.0-2.3%
**TIPS liquidity:** breakevens can be distorted by liquidity premia during stress
**Survey cross-check:** Michigan and SPF forecasts provide independent verification

moderate.formal: Breakeven = nominal yield - TIPS real yield = expected inflation + inflation risk premium.

expert.bluf: Breakeven = expected inflation + inflation risk premium (IRP). The IRP is time-varying (20-50bp), making breakevens biased. Kim-Wright decomposition separates the components. TIPS indexation lag and liquidity premia add further noise.

sections.head: Why it matters
sections.body: The IRP was historically positive but turned negative during QE. Current estimates (~30-50bp) suggest breakevens overstate true expectations by that amount.

sections.head: What to watch
body: **Kim-Wright decomposition:** the Fed's reference model
**TIPS liquidity premium:** during stress can spike 50-100bp, collapsing breakevens even as expectations rise
**CPI-PCE wedge:** TIPS index to CPI but Fed targets PCE - ~30bp systematic gap

expert.formal: Breakeven = E[pi] + IRP + liquidity adjustment. 5Y5Y forward: [(1+BE10)^10/(1+BE5)^5]^(1/5) - 1.

beginner.bluf: A recession is when an economy shrinks for a sustained period. People lose jobs, businesses close, and spending falls. The informal rule of thumb is two consecutive quarters of falling GDP, though the official definition is broader.

sections.head: Why it matters
sections.body: Recessions cause real hardship - unemployment rises, wages stagnate, businesses fail, and government finances deteriorate. Stocks typically fall 20-30%, bond yields drop as central banks cut rates, and currencies of affected countries weaken.

sections.head: Example
sections.body: The COVID recession (2020) was the deepest in modern history but the shortest (2 months). The 2008 financial crisis lasted 18 months. The Great Depression lasted over 3 years. Each had very different causes and recovery patterns.

beginner.formal: A significant, widespread, and prolonged decline in economic activity, typically visible in GDP, employment, income, and industrial production.

moderate.bluf: A broad-based contraction officially dated by the NBER based on depth, diffusion, and duration. The two-quarter GDP rule is a rough shortcut. Leading indicators (yield curve, PMIs, credit) typically signal recessions 6-12 months in advance.

sections.head: Why it matters
sections.body: Recessions are the key regime changes for asset allocation. Equities peak 6-9 months before the recession starts. Bonds rally as central banks cut. Credit spreads widen.

sections.head: What to watch
body: **Yield curve:** 3m-10Y and 2Y-10Y inversions have preceded every US recession since 1970
**Sahm Rule:** 0.5pp rise in 3-month average unemployment from its 12-month low
**PMI below 50:** manufacturing PMI sustained below 48-49 is consistent with recession

moderate.formal: A significant decline in activity spread across the economy lasting more than a few months. Median post-WWII US recession: 10 months, 2.5% peak-to-trough GDP decline.

expert.bluf: Recessions are nonlinear regime transitions. Probit models using the yield curve, credit conditions, and labour data give probabilistic forecasts, but false positives are increasing as structural changes alter signal-to-noise ratios.

sections.head: Why it matters
sections.body: The recession/expansion binary is the most consequential macro call. Asset returns are bimodal: equities average -25% during recessions vs +15% during expansions. Real-time identification relies on nowcasting models whose reliability varies across cycles.

sections.head: What to watch
body: **Regime-switching models:** Hamilton Markov-switching and Chauvet-Piger smoothed probabilities
**Near-term forward spread:** Engstrom-Sharpe's measure has better signal-to-noise than 2s10s
**Soft landing rarity:** the Fed has achieved it only 3 times since 1965

expert.formal: A nonlinear regime shift from expansion to contraction. Hamilton Markov-switching models estimate transition probabilities using observable macro variables.

beginner.bluf: When an economy stops growing but doesn't necessarily shrink. A period of little or no economic progress.

moderate.bluf: Prolonged period of low or zero growth. Japan's 'Lost Decades' (1990s-2010s) is the canonical example. Secular stagnation hypothesis (Summers 2014) suggested advanced economies face structurally low growth and rates.

expert.bluf: Persistent sub-potential growth. Secular stagnation thesis attributes it to excess saving, demographic drag, and declining marginal productivity of capital. Japan's experience (30+ years) includes debt overhang, zombie firms, and demographic decline. Policy responses - fiscal expansion and structural reform - are politically difficult to sustain.

beginner.bluf: When inflation slows down but remains positive - prices are still rising, just not as fast. Disinflation is not deflation. If inflation falls from 8% to 3%, that is disinflation: things still get more expensive, but the pace has slowed.

sections.head: Why it matters
sections.body: Disinflation is what central banks aim for when they raise rates to fight high inflation. They want to bring it down to ~2% without crashing the economy. The process determines when central banks can stop hiking and start cutting.

sections.head: Example
sections.body: US inflation peaked at 9.1% in June 2022 and fell to about 3% by mid-2024. Prices were still going up - just more slowly. The last stretch from 3% to 2% proved the hardest.

beginner.formal: A decline in the rate of inflation - prices continue to rise but at a decreasing rate.

moderate.bluf: A falling inflation rate that remains positive. Goods disinflation is typically fast (supply normalisation), while services disinflation is slow and sticky (wages). The "last mile" from 3% to 2% is the most difficult.

sections.head: Why it matters
sections.body: Speed and composition determine the policy path. Rapid, broad disinflation allows early cuts. Slow, narrow disinflation forces rates higher for longer.

sections.head: What to watch
body: **Goods vs services:** goods disinflation is largely done; services is the battleground
**Supercore:** core services ex-housing needs to fall to ~3% annualised
**Base effects:** large price increases rolling off create mechanical disinflation

moderate.formal: A declining inflation rate (delta-pi < 0 while pi > 0). Sacrifice ratio: 1.5-3.0 typically.

expert.bluf: Disinflation is the policy objective post-inflation shock. The sacrifice ratio and speed of expectations re-anchoring determine soft-landing odds. The nonlinearity - fast then slow - creates a timing trap for central banks.

sections.head: Why it matters
sections.body: The sacrifice ratio this cycle appears low (~0.5) because much disinflation came from supply healing rather than demand destruction.

sections.head: What to watch
body: **Sacrifice ratio:** cumulative unemployment rise per pp of disinflation - historically 1.5-3.0, lower this cycle
**Immaculate disinflation:** inflation returning to target without recession - supported so far but rare
**Persistence:** trimmed mean, median CPI, and MCT reveal momentum better than headline

expert.formal: Declining inflation. Sacrifice ratio = cumulative output gap / cumulative disinflation.

beginner.bluf: The difference between what an economy is actually producing and what it could produce at full capacity. Positive means overheating; negative means underperformance.

moderate.bluf: Gap between actual and potential GDP. Positive gap (above potential) creates inflation pressure; negative gap means slack. Central banks use it to calibrate monetary policy. The challenge: potential GDP is unobservable and estimates are revised significantly.

expert.bluf: Y − Y* expressed as percentage of potential. Central to Taylor Rule calibration but subject to substantial real-time measurement error (Orphanides 2001) - initial estimates revised by 1-2pp on average. HP filter, production function, and multivariate (Kalman filter) approaches yield divergent estimates. Policy errors from misestimating the output gap are a recurring historical pattern.

beginner.bluf: The maximum amount an economy can produce sustainably without causing excessive inflation. It's the economy's 'speed limit.'

moderate.bluf: Maximum sustainable output at full employment without accelerating inflation. Determined by labour force, capital stock, and productivity (total factor productivity). Structural reforms aim to raise potential GDP over time.

expert.bluf: Supply-side concept: Y* = f(L*, K, TFP). Unobservable; estimated via production function, HP filter, or state-space models. Post-pandemic: potential GDP estimates highly uncertain due to labour market structural shifts, capital reallocation, and AI-driven productivity changes. Long-run growth ≈ labour force growth + productivity growth.

beginner.bluf: The total value of everything a country produces - all goods and services - adjusted for inflation. The 'real' part means we strip out price increases so we can see whether the economy actually produced more stuff, not just charged more for the same amount.

sections.head: Why it matters
sections.body: Real GDP is the standard measure of an economy's size and health. It tells you whether a country is producing more goods and delivering more services than before. Without adjusting for inflation, you might think the economy grew when really prices just went up.

sections.head: Intuition
sections.body: Imagine a baker who made 100 loaves last year at $2 each ($200 revenue) and 100 loaves this year at $3 each ($300 revenue). Nominal GDP says output grew 50%. Real GDP says 0% - same number of loaves. Real GDP tells the truth about actual production.

beginner.formal: Gross Domestic Product adjusted for inflation, measuring the total value of goods and services produced within a country, expressed in constant prices of a base year.

moderate.bluf: GDP deflated by a price index to measure volume change, not price change. Chain-weighted methodology avoids substitution bias. Real GDP growth is the headline measure of performance, but nominal GDP matters more for debt sustainability and corporate revenue.

sections.head: Why it matters
sections.body: Real GDP is the denominator in debt-to-GDP, the driver of tax revenue, and the benchmark against which potential output is measured. The output gap is the key input into inflation forecasting and monetary policy.

sections.head: What to watch
body: **Nominal vs real:** for debt sustainability and corporate revenue, nominal GDP is what matters
**Chain weighting:** modern GDP uses annually updated weights - components do not sum to the total
**Revisions:** initial GDP estimates are revised significantly

moderate.formal: GDP measured in constant prices using chain-weighted deflation. Expenditure: C + I + G + (X - M), each deflated by component-specific price indices.

expert.bluf: Real GDP is the chain-weighted volume measure of aggregate output. It is an imperfect welfare proxy (excludes non-market activity, leisure, environmental costs) and an imperfect cycle indicator (GDI divergences, residual seasonality, benchmark revisions).

sections.head: Why it matters
sections.body: The GDP-GDI gap averages 0.5pp in any quarter and can exceed 2pp - averaging the two is more accurate. Residual seasonality in Q1 US GDP creates a persistent downward bias. Benchmark revisions can change the narrative - the 2008 recession was initially -0.5% and later revised to -2.5%.

sections.head: What to watch
body: **GDP-GDI average:** the best single measure of current output growth
**Benchmark revisions:** annual comprehensive revisions can change the narrative entirely
**Real GDI:** better at capturing the income side that drives spending

expert.formal: Chain-weighted real GDP: geometric mean of Laspeyres and Paasche volume indices. Expenditure-income statistical discrepancy averages ~0.5pp quarterly.

beginner.bluf: The idea that there's a trade-off between unemployment and inflation - when unemployment is very low, inflation tends to rise, and vice versa.

moderate.bluf: Inverse relationship between unemployment and inflation. Originally (1958) an empirical observation; now a core macro model component. The curve has 'flattened' in recent decades - inflation became less responsive to unemployment - but may steepen at very low unemployment levels.

expert.bluf: Expectations-augmented Phillips Curve: π = πe + α(u* − u) + supply shocks. New Keynesian Phillips Curve derives from Calvo pricing. Slope has flattened (globalisation, anchored expectations) but exhibits nonlinearity - steepens materially below ~4% unemployment. Debate on whether the curve has 'died' or is merely dormant; post-COVID inflation resurgence suggests the relationship remains alive at extremes.

beginner.bluf: A dangerous cycle where workers demand higher wages because prices are rising, which forces businesses to raise prices further, which triggers more wage demands.

moderate.bluf: Self-reinforcing loop: high inflation → higher wage demands → increased business costs → further price increases → higher inflation expectations. Central banks raise rates aggressively to break the spiral by reducing demand. Risks are highest when inflation expectations become 'unanchored.'

expert.bluf: Second-round effect where inflation feeds into wage bargaining, which feeds back into costs and prices. The spiral requires sustained real wage claims exceeding productivity growth. Historical examples: 1970s US/UK. Modern risk assessed via unit labour cost growth, inflation expectations surveys, and wage Phillips Curve slopes. Credible inflation targeting is the primary preventive mechanism.

beginner.bluf: When companies and households all focus on paying down debt instead of spending or investing, causing a prolonged economic slump even when interest rates are very low.

moderate.bluf: Theory (Richard Koo) explaining Japan's Lost Decades: after an asset bubble bursts, private sector shifts from profit maximisation to debt minimisation. Even at zero rates, no one borrows - fiscal policy is the only effective stimulus.

expert.bluf: Koo (2003) framework: post-bubble private sector deleveraging creates paradox of thrift at aggregate level. Monetary policy impotent as credit demand absent. Fiscal policy is the only effective stabiliser - premature consolidation prolongs the downturn (Japan 1997, eurozone 2011-12). Requires sustained fiscal deficits until private balance sheets are repaired.

beginner.bluf: Ben Bernanke's theory that a flood of savings from Asia and oil-exporting countries flowed into the US, pushing down interest rates and contributing to the housing bubble.

moderate.bluf: Bernanke's (2005) hypothesis: excess saving in Asia (particularly China) and oil exporters depressed global interest rates by flooding capital into US Treasuries. This external factor, rather than Fed policy alone, explained low long-term rates. Remains relevant for understanding global imbalances.

expert.bluf: Bernanke thesis attributing low global rates to ex ante saving exceeding investment in Asia and OPEC. Counterpoint: Borio-Disyatat (2011) argue financing (gross flows) matters more than saving (net flows). The savings glut framework underpins the 'global imbalances' narrative and partially explains the pre-2008 credit boom.

beginner.bluf: The most dangerous stage of borrowing - when a borrower can only pay their debts by taking on even more debt. Named by economist Hyman Minsky.

moderate.bluf: Final stage in Minsky's financial instability hypothesis. Borrowers can neither pay interest nor principal from income - they rely on asset appreciation or new borrowing to stay solvent. When refinancing stops, collapse follows.

expert.bluf: Third stage of Minsky's taxonomy (hedge → speculative → Ponzi). Cash flows insufficient to cover even interest payments; unit depends on asset price appreciation or refinancing for solvency. System-wide Ponzi dynamics indicate fragility approaching the Minsky moment. China's LGFV sector exhibits Ponzi characteristics where land revenue declines have eliminated the income base.

beginner.bluf: A broad measure of how easy or hard it is to borrow money and access funding in the economy - influenced by interest rates, stock prices, credit spreads, and the dollar.

moderate.bluf: Composite gauge of the tightness or ease of the financial environment. Financial conditions indices (Goldman Sachs FCI, Chicago Fed NFCI) aggregate interest rates, credit spreads, equity prices, FX, and volatility into a single measure. Looser conditions = easier access to credit and funding.

expert.bluf: Multi-factor index aggregating rates, spreads, equities, FX, and vol. Impulse from financial conditions to real economy has ~3-6 quarter lag. The Fed implicitly targets financial conditions through the 'financial conditions channel' - market reactions to policy/guidance adjust conditions beyond the direct rate change. FCI tightening without rate hikes (e.g., via spread widening) can substitute for policy tightening.

beginner.bluf: Japan's annual 'spring wage offensive' - a coordinated round of wage negotiations between unions and employers that sets the tone for pay across the economy.

moderate.bluf: Japan's annual spring wage negotiations between unions and major employers. The 2024 round delivered 3.6% - the highest since 1993. Critical for BOJ policy: sustained wage growth is the prerequisite for normalising monetary policy away from ultra-ease.

expert.bluf: Annual spring labour offensive; results signal economy-wide wage dynamics in Japan's coordinated wage-setting system. 2024 Shunto at 3.6% (highest since 1993) was the key data point enabling BOJ NIRP exit. Transmission to smaller firms and real wage positivity (nominal wages > CPI) is the sustainability test.

beginner.bluf: A monthly survey of financial experts about their expectations for the German economy. An early indicator of economic direction.

moderate.bluf: ZEW Economic Sentiment indicator: monthly survey of ~350 financial analysts' expectations for the German economy (6-month outlook). More forward-looking than Ifo (which surveys actual businesses). Often diverges from Ifo at turning points.

expert.bluf: Survey-based expectations index from the Leibniz Centre for European Economic Research. Leads Ifo by ~2 months at turning points. Current ZEW-Ifo divergence (expectations recovering faster than current conditions) historically signals trough formation, though structural headwinds may limit the cyclical recovery.

beginner.bluf: Inflation is a sustained increase in the overall price level of goods and services, which reduces the purchasing power of money over time. When inflation rises, each unit of currency buys fewer things.

sections.head: Why it matters
sections.body: Inflation affects how far wages go, how savings lose or keep value, how interest rates are set, and how governments and central banks make policy. Too much inflation erodes trust in money; too little can signal economic stagnation.

sections.head: Intuition / context
sections.body: Think of money as a measuring stick for value. Inflation means the stick is slowly shrinking. Prices aren't just going up randomly - the value of money itself is going down relative to goods and services across the economy.

sections.head: Example
sections.body: If a basket of everyday items costs $100 this year and $103 next year, the inflation rate is 3%. If your income didn't rise by at least 3%, you're effectively poorer, even though your paycheck is the same in dollar terms.

sections.head: What inflation is not
body: A one-time price increase for a single good
The same thing as "high prices" (inflation is about change, not level)
Always caused by greed or shortages alone

sections.head: Common causes
body: **Demand-pull:** too much spending chasing too few goods
**Cost-push:** rising production costs passed to consumers
**Monetary factors:** growth in the money supply faster than real output

beginner.formal: Inflation is the rate of change of a general price index (such as the Consumer Price Index) over time.

moderate.bluf: Inflation is the sustained rate of increase in the general price level, measured by indices like CPI or PCE. Central banks target ~2% as the sweet spot - high enough to avoid the zero lower bound, low enough to preserve purchasing power.

sections.head: Why it matters
sections.body: Inflation determines real interest rates, erodes nominal debt burdens, affects wage negotiations, and is the primary variable central banks target. It transmits directly to bond yields, FX, and equity valuations.

sections.head: Intuition / context
sections.body: Inflation is the economy's temperature gauge. Moderate inflation signals healthy demand. Too high means overheating. Deflation (negative inflation) is often worse than moderate inflation because it increases the real burden of debt and delays consumption.

sections.head: Example
sections.body: US CPI at 3.1% means the consumer price basket rose 3.1% year-over-year. Core CPI strips out volatile food and energy to reveal the underlying trend. The Fed watches core PCE (not CPI) as its preferred gauge.

sections.head: Often confused with
body: **Price level** - inflation is the rate of *change*, not how expensive things are
**CPI** - CPI is one index that measures inflation, not inflation itself
**Deflation** - not just "low inflation" but sustained negative price changes

sections.head: Key types
body: **Headline:** all items including food and energy
**Core:** excludes food and energy - the Fed's focus
**Supercore:** core services excluding housing - the "last mile" measure

moderate.formal: The percentage change in a broad consumer price index over a defined period, typically expressed year-over-year.

expert.bluf: Inflation is the rate of change of the general price level. Operationally, the distinction between headline, core, trimmed mean, and supercore measures is critical - each captures different persistence dynamics and has different policy signal content.

sections.head: Why it matters
sections.body: Inflation expectations anchoring is the central bank's most valuable asset. De-anchoring triggers nonlinear policy responses. The real interest rate (nominal minus expected inflation) drives all asset pricing, investment decisions, and currency valuation.

sections.head: Intuition / context
sections.body: Inflation is ultimately a monetary phenomenon in the long run (Friedman), but in the short run, supply shocks, expectations, and labour market tightness all matter. The Phillips Curve slope is nonlinear - flat at moderate unemployment, steep below ~4%.

sections.head: Example
sections.body: Post-COVID US: headline CPI peaked at 9.1% (June 2022). Goods disinflation was rapid (supply chains), but services inflation - particularly shelter and core services ex-housing (supercore) - proved sticky. The "last mile" from 3% to 2% required 500bp of tightening and 18+ months of lag.

sections.head: Often confused with
body: **CPI vs PCE:** PCE uses Fisher weighting (substitution-adjusted), broader scope, typically 30-40bps below CPI
**Breakevens vs expectations:** TIPS breakevens include an inflation risk premium, not pure expectations
**Transitory vs persistent:** trimmed mean and median CPI better identify persistence than core

sections.head: Measurement nuances
body: **Boskin bias:** CPI overstates inflation by ~0.5-1pp (substitution, quality, new goods effects)
**Shelter lag:** OER/rent of shelter lags market rents by 12-18 months - distorts turning points
**Trimmed mean:** Dallas Fed 16% trimmed mean is the best real-time persistence signal

expert.formal: The rate of change of a general price index. Operationally: π = ΔP/P, where measurement methodology (Laspeyres vs Fisher, scope, quality adjustment) materially affects the signal.

beginner.bluf: The lowest unemployment rate an economy can sustain without triggering rising inflation.

moderate.bluf: Non-Accelerating Inflation Rate of Unemployment - the structural unemployment rate below which inflation tends to accelerate. Estimated at ~4.0-4.5% for the US. Central to policy calibration.

expert.bluf: Unobservable equilibrium concept. Time-varying due to hysteresis, demographic shifts, and labour market structural change. CBO estimates ~4.4% for the US. Phillips Curve nonlinearity means NAIRU is not a cliff - inflation acceleration is gradual above it, steep below it. Real-time estimation error is substantial.

beginner.bluf: The share of working-age people who are either employed or actively looking for a job.

moderate.bluf: Percentage of the working-age population in the labour force (employed + unemployed). Falling participation alongside falling unemployment can indicate discouraged workers exiting, not a strengthening job market.

expert.bluf: LFPR decomposition by age, gender, and education reveals structural vs cyclical dynamics. Prime-age (25-54) participation is the cleanest signal. US LFPR decline partly structural (ageing) but COVID caused an additional ~1pp drop in prime-age that has only partially recovered. India's low female LFPR (~25%) is a structural growth constraint.

beginner.bluf: A recession indicator that triggers when unemployment rises quickly - specifically, when the 3-month average jumps half a percentage point above its recent low.

moderate.bluf: Real-time recession indicator: when the 3-month moving average of the US unemployment rate rises 0.5pp or more above its 12-month low, a recession has historically already begun. Named after economist Claudia Sahm.

expert.bluf: Empirical recession identification rule with perfect historical track record (100% accuracy since 1970). Advantage over yield curve inversion: identifies recession in real-time rather than with a lead. The 0.5pp threshold reflects nonlinear labour market dynamics - small rises in unemployment tend to snowball as income losses reduce spending, causing further layoffs.

beginner.bluf: GDP Growth measures how fast a country's economy is expanding or shrinking. It is the single most important number for understanding whether an economy is healthy, struggling, or in recession.

sections.head: Why it matters
sections.body: GDP Growth tells you whether there are more jobs being created, more goods being produced, and more income being earned than before. Governments, businesses, and investors all watch this number closely because it affects everything from tax revenue to corporate profits to your chances of getting a raise.

sections.head: Intuition
sections.body: Think of the economy as a pie. GDP Growth tells you whether the pie is getting bigger or smaller. A growing pie means more to go around for everyone. A shrinking pie - recession - means painful choices about who gets less.

sections.head: Example
sections.body: If a country's GDP grew 2.5% this year, it means the total value of everything the economy produced went up by 2.5% compared to last year. If you earned $50,000 last year and the economy grew 2.5%, there is more national income to support wage growth, new hiring, and business expansion.

sections.head: What to watch
body: Growth above 3% in developed economies is strong - it typically means falling unemployment and rising wages
Growth near 0% signals stagnation - the economy is barely treading water
Negative growth for two consecutive quarters is the informal definition of a recession
China and India grow faster (4-7%) because they are catching up from lower starting points

beginner.formal: The annualised percentage change in real (inflation-adjusted) Gross Domestic Product over a given period.

moderate.bluf: GDP Growth is the annualised change in real output. It drives corporate earnings trajectories, fiscal arithmetic, employment, and is the macro variable most correlated with risk asset performance across cycles.

sections.head: Why it matters
sections.body: GDP growth is the numerator in almost every macro ratio that matters - debt-to-GDP, deficit-to-GDP, earnings growth. Above-trend growth compresses credit spreads, supports equity multiples, and gives central banks room to normalise rates. Below-trend growth does the opposite. The growth rate also determines whether fiscal deficits are sustainable (the r-g dynamic).

sections.head: Intuition
sections.body: Growth is the economy's velocity. It determines whether the debt burden is rising or falling in real terms, whether tax receipts are expanding, and whether corporate top-line revenue growth is achievable. A 1% GDP miss typically translates to a 2-3% miss in earnings growth via operating leverage.

sections.head: Example
sections.body: US GDP grew 2.5% in 2024 despite 525bp of cumulative rate hikes - a textbook soft landing. This above-trend growth supported S&P 500 earnings growth of ~8% and kept the unemployment rate below 4%. Contrast with Germany at 0.2% - near stagnation - where the DAX lagged and fiscal pressures mounted.

sections.head: What to watch
body: **Output gap:** actual vs potential GDP - positive gap means overheating, negative means slack
**Composition:** consumption-led growth is stickier than inventory-led growth
**Revisions:** GDP data gets revised heavily - the first print is a rough estimate
**Leading indicators:** PMIs, yield curve slope, and credit growth all lead GDP by 6-12 months

moderate.formal: The annualised percentage change in real GDP, typically reported quarterly with advance, second, and third estimates subject to significant revision.

expert.bluf: Real GDP growth is the broadest measure of aggregate output change. The r-g differential (real rate vs real growth) is the key structural variable for debt sustainability, while the output gap drives inflation dynamics via the Phillips Curve.

sections.head: Why it matters
sections.body: Growth is the denominator that makes everything else work. When g > r, debt-to-GDP ratios stabilise even with primary deficits. When r > g, fiscal consolidation becomes mathematically necessary. For markets, the growth-rate transition (acceleration vs deceleration) matters more than the level - equities price the second derivative.

sections.head: Intuition
sections.body: Potential growth is the economy's speed limit - determined by demographics (labour force growth), capital deepening, and TFP. Actual growth oscillates around potential. The gap between them is what central banks really target, since it maps to inflation pressure via the Phillips Curve. Secular stagnation thesis: potential growth has structurally declined across DM (from ~3% to ~1.5-2%) due to demographics and slowing productivity.

sections.head: Example
sections.body: Japan's nominal GDP was roughly flat for two decades (1995-2015) despite massive fiscal stimulus, because deflation offset real growth. The lesson: nominal GDP growth (real + inflation) is what actually matters for debt dynamics, tax revenue, and corporate top-line. Abenomics targeted nominal GDP explicitly for this reason.

sections.head: What to watch
body: **GDI vs GDP:** gross domestic income should equal GDP but divergences signal measurement noise - trust the average
**Residual seasonality:** Q1 GDP in the US is systematically biased downward
**Nowcasting:** Atlanta Fed GDPNow and NY Fed nowcast are real-time tracking estimates worth following
**Nominal vs real:** for debt sustainability and corporate revenue, nominal GDP growth is the relevant metric

expert.formal: The annualised rate of change in chain-weighted real GDP. Measurement: expenditure approach (C + I + G + NX) or income approach (GDI). The statistical discrepancy between the two averages ~0.5pp in any given quarter.

beginner.bluf: The unemployment rate measures what percentage of people who want to work cannot find a job. It is one of the clearest signals of whether an economy is providing enough opportunity for its citizens.

sections.head: Why it matters
sections.body: Unemployment directly affects living standards, consumer spending, government finances, and social stability. High unemployment means wasted potential - people who could be contributing to the economy are sitting idle. It also means lower tax revenue and higher welfare spending for governments.

sections.head: Intuition
sections.body: Think of the economy as a team. The unemployment rate tells you how many players are on the bench who want to be in the game. Some bench-sitting is normal (people between jobs), but too much means the team is underperforming.

sections.head: Example
sections.body: An unemployment rate of 4% means that out of every 100 people looking for work, 4 cannot find a job. In the US, anything below 4% is considered very tight - employers struggle to find workers, and wages tend to rise faster.

sections.head: What to watch
body: Below 4% in the US or UK signals a tight labour market - good for workers, potentially inflationary
Above 7-8% signals real distress - demand is too weak to employ everyone
Youth unemployment is often 2-3x the headline rate and can signal deeper structural problems
The rate can fall for bad reasons - people stop looking for work and drop out of the count

beginner.formal: The percentage of the labour force (those employed plus those actively seeking work) that is unemployed.

moderate.bluf: Unemployment is a lagging indicator that reflects labour market slack. Central banks watch it alongside wages and participation to gauge how much capacity remains before inflation accelerates - the Phillips Curve trade-off.

sections.head: Why it matters
sections.body: The unemployment rate is half of the Fed's dual mandate (alongside price stability). It drives consumer spending (70% of US GDP), wage growth dynamics, and determines how much room central banks have to keep rates elevated. A rising unemployment rate is the most reliable recession signal and the trigger for rate cuts.

sections.head: Intuition
sections.body: Unemployment is a lagging indicator - it rises after a recession has already begun and falls after recovery is underway. But the rate of change matters more than the level. The Sahm Rule: if the 3-month moving average of unemployment rises 0.5pp above its 12-month low, the economy is already in recession 100% of the time historically.

sections.head: Example
sections.body: US unemployment hit 3.4% in early 2023 - a 53-year low. This ultra-tight market fuelled 5%+ wage growth, which fed into services inflation. The Fed needed unemployment to rise toward 4-4.5% to ease wage pressure. The question was whether this could happen without a recession (soft landing) or not (hard landing).

sections.head: What to watch
body: **U-3 vs U-6:** U-3 is the headline rate; U-6 includes discouraged workers and part-time for economic reasons - a broader measure of slack
**Participation rate:** a falling unemployment rate with falling participation is not a healthy signal
**JOLTS:** job openings and quits rate show labour demand and worker confidence
**Sahm Rule:** 0.5pp rise from the trough in 3-month average triggers recession signal

moderate.formal: The U-3 unemployment rate: the number of unemployed persons actively seeking work, divided by the civilian labour force, expressed as a percentage.

expert.bluf: The unemployment rate is a lagging, survey-based measure of labour slack. NAIRU estimation, the Beveridge Curve, and the distinction between U-3 and broader measures (U-6, prime-age EPOP) are essential for assessing true tightness.

sections.head: Why it matters
sections.body: The gap between actual unemployment and NAIRU (the non-accelerating inflation rate of unemployment) is the labour market's contribution to inflation dynamics. Post-COVID, NAIRU estimates have been unreliable - the Beveridge Curve shifted outward (more vacancies per unit of unemployment), suggesting matching efficiency declined, then partially recovered.

sections.head: Intuition
sections.body: The unemployment rate is a noisy signal of slack. The household survey (which generates unemployment) and the establishment survey (which generates payrolls) frequently diverge. Prime-age employment-to-population ratio (25-54 EPOP) is a cleaner measure of labour utilisation because it is unaffected by participation definition issues and demographic shifts.

sections.head: Example
sections.body: Post-COVID labour market: US unemployment fell from 14.7% (April 2020) to 3.4% (January 2023) - the fastest decline on record. But participation remained 1pp below pre-COVID levels, and the Beveridge Curve showed structurally higher vacancies per unemployed worker. This meant the headline rate understated actual tightness relative to historical norms.

sections.head: What to watch
body: **Sahm Rule:** 0.5pp rise in 3-month average from 12-month trough - perfect recession predictor historically
**JOLTS quits rate:** the best real-time indicator of worker bargaining power and wage pressure
**Beveridge Curve:** the vacancy-unemployment relationship reveals matching efficiency changes
**Birth-death model:** BLS business birth-death adjustment adds phantom jobs in downturns - trust benchmark revisions

expert.formal: The ratio of unemployed persons (defined as jobless, available for work, and actively seeking employment in the prior 4 weeks) to the civilian labour force. Subject to household survey sampling noise of approximately +/-100k per month.

beginner.bluf: The budget deficit measures how much more a government spends than it earns in a given year. A deficit means the government is borrowing to cover the gap, adding to national debt.

sections.head: Why it matters
sections.body: Deficits determine how much a government needs to borrow. Persistent large deficits mean growing national debt, which eventually means higher interest payments, higher taxes, or reduced public services. Markets watch deficits closely because they affect bond supply, interest rates, and confidence in a country's finances.

sections.head: Intuition
sections.body: Think of it like a household budget. If you earn $4,000 a month but spend $5,000, you have a $1,000 deficit. You cover it with a credit card (borrowing). One month is fine - but if you do it every month for years, the interest payments start eating into your spending. Governments work the same way, just with more zeros.

sections.head: Example
sections.body: A budget deficit of -6% of GDP means the government spent 6% more than the entire economy's annual output in extra borrowing. The US deficit has averaged around -5% to -7% of GDP in recent years - historically high for a peacetime economy not in recession.

sections.head: What to watch
body: Deficits below -3% of GDP are generally considered manageable for developed economies
Deficits above -6% outside of recessions signal structural overspending
Deficits matter more when interest rates are high - borrowing costs compound
A surplus (positive number) is rare and means the government is paying down debt

beginner.formal: Government revenue minus government expenditure, expressed as a percentage of GDP. A negative number indicates a deficit (spending exceeds revenue).

moderate.bluf: The fiscal deficit as a percentage of GDP measures structural and cyclical government borrowing needs. It drives bond supply, affects term premia, and determines the trajectory of debt-to-GDP - the key solvency metric.

sections.head: Why it matters
sections.body: The deficit is the flow that drives the debt stock. Large deficits increase bond issuance, which can push up term premia and crowd out private investment. The sustainability question hinges on whether nominal GDP growth exceeds the effective interest rate on debt (the r-g framework). When deficits are large and r > g, debt-to-GDP spirals upward.

sections.head: Intuition
sections.body: Deficits are not inherently bad - during recessions, automatic stabilisers (falling tax revenue, rising welfare spending) widen the deficit to cushion the economy. The concern is structural deficits - persistent borrowing even when the economy is at full employment. That signals a political inability to match spending with revenue.

sections.head: Example
sections.body: The US ran a ~6.5% deficit in 2024 despite sub-4% unemployment - unprecedented in peacetime at full employment. This deficit was driven by interest payments (~3.5% of GDP), defence, and entitlements. Bond market concerns about supply pushed the 10Y yield above 4.5%, effectively tightening financial conditions from the fiscal side.

sections.head: What to watch
body: **Primary deficit:** deficit excluding interest payments - shows the discretionary fiscal stance
**Cyclically adjusted:** structural deficit removes automatic stabilisers - the true policy choice
**Interest expense ratio:** interest payments as % of revenue - above 15% starts constraining fiscal flexibility
**Bond auction demand:** weak bid-to-cover ratios signal market fatigue with supply

moderate.formal: General government net lending/borrowing as a percentage of GDP. Negative values indicate a deficit. The structural (cyclically adjusted) deficit strips out automatic stabiliser effects.

expert.bluf: The fiscal deficit is the flow variable driving debt dynamics. The key identity: change in debt-to-GDP = (r-g) x existing debt ratio + primary deficit. At current DM debt levels, the r-g sign determines whether consolidation is arithmetically necessary.

sections.head: Why it matters
sections.body: Fiscal dominance risk has re-emerged. When debt-to-GDP exceeds ~100%, the deficit-interest payment feedback loop becomes self-reinforcing if r > g. The US is running 6%+ deficits at full employment with net interest approaching 4% of GDP. This is the bond market's central concern and the driver of term premium repricing since 2023.

sections.head: Intuition
sections.body: The debt dynamics equation is unforgiving: d(debt/GDP)/dt = (r-g)(debt/GDP) - primary surplus. When debt/GDP is 120% (US) and r-g is +1%, you need a 1.2% primary surplus just to stabilise - before any new spending. The US currently runs a ~3% primary deficit. The math requires either much faster growth, much lower rates, or fiscal consolidation that no political coalition will deliver.

sections.head: Example
sections.body: Italy (debt/GDP ~140%) survived the 2010s because ECB policy kept r far below g. With ECB tightening, Italian BTP spreads widened to 250bp as markets priced the return of debt sustainability risk. The Transmission Protection Instrument (TPI) was explicitly created to prevent deficit concerns from fragmenting the euro area - fiscal backstopped by monetary.

sections.head: What to watch
